overview: This record begins while Montenegro was still joined with Serbia. A referendum in 2006 led to a separate independent republic. The modern outline therefore crosses a major change in sovereignty; it should not imply that Montenegro was already independent in 1994. Its families, coastal associations and northern farming communities continued through that change.

periods.title: Within a shared state
periods.summary: Montenegro remained joined with Serbia, latterly in the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro.

periods.title: Independent republic
periods.summary: The referendum led to a declaration of independence on 3 June 2006.

items.text: The Boka Navy of Kotor preserves seafaring traditions through a voluntary cultural association. Membership is open to men, women and children. Its modern work commemorates maritime life and brings generations together, rather than functioning as a present-day combat navy.

At formal celebrations, members wear colourful traditional uniforms, carry historic weapons and perform the kolo circle dance. The coordinated steps make a public ceremony out of inherited movement and dress. Historic objects become part of a performance in the town’s shared spaces.

The association transmits knowledge of maritime history, customs and traditional skills. Younger participants learn through involvement with older members. Its heritage includes people remembering and practising together, alongside the uniforms and objects that can be displayed in a museum.

The Preschool for All campaign began in March 2015 in five northern municipalities with particularly low attendance. UNICEF and the education ministry worked with local preschools and communities. Some places had available classroom capacity but needed stronger connections with families.

Arts and educational events invited parents and young children to experience preschool activities. Partners included drama, music and ballet institutions, as well as teacher educators. Learning through songs, movement and play could help families picture what a preschool day offered.

The campaign expanded to six more northern municipalities in 2016. Its posters show children painting, shaping clay, reading picture books and playing. These surviving campaign materials document the everyday activities used to explain early learning to the public.

At the 2017 Days of Pljevlja Cheese, producers presented cheeses and cream for judging, tasting and sale. Around a hundred producers submitted 172 samples. The event connected household and farm production with customers beyond an individual village.

Pljevlja cheese received national protection of its origin in 2017. The event included producers from the wider cross-border Drina-Tara region as well as Montenegro. A named local food could support both a sense of place and practical cooperation between farming communities.

Article 1 of the constitution begins “Crna Gora je nezavisna i suverena država”, meaning “Montenegro is an independent and sovereign state”. This attested Montenegrin sentence uses Latin letters. The constitution was adopted in October 2007, after the independence referendum.

The constitution gives Cyrillic and Latin scripts equal status and identifies several languages in official use. A country’s written life can therefore use more than one alphabet. These provisions concern public institutions, alongside the languages used within individual households.

The 2007 constitution also describes the state as ecological and committed to social justice. Such language sets out constitutional goals. It records how lawmakers defined the republic, rather than proving that every environmental or social problem had been solved.

In the May 2006 referendum, 55.5 percent of valid votes supported independence. The result led to the June declaration. The vote also shows that citizens held different views about their state’s future, even as the new republic’s institutions took shape.

ending.text: The union with Serbia ended for Montenegro in 2006, and the independent republic continued. This was a change in sovereignty, not an ending of the country’s communities or cultural life.
